comment: Where each fact about these parts stands, given that the ROM is the part and the interface around it is not documented.

sources.microcode: The program masked into each part's ROM, run rather than described. Supplied by whoever holds it; nothing is carried here.
sources.document: NEC's uPD77C25 data sheet covers the smaller processor. No document for the uPD96050 was located.
sources.reference: The behavioural models in emulators, which is where the interface constants come from.

divergences.documentSays: Nothing about how a console gets these parts' attention.
divergences.referenceDoes: Derived models describe eight commands and account for a write that none of them explains, which is usually handled by treating an address as an enable switch.
divergences.reasoning: On the part there is no switch. Running the program shows what actually happens: it raises its attention bit on its very first instruction and waits for the console to take a word off the data port, and until that happens it never reaches the loop that watches for a command. A part spoken to without it answers nothing and reads as broken. This is the case that justifies the whole approach: a derived model covers the commands somebody thought to look at, and this was in none of them.
divergences.wouldReopenIt: Finding an image whose program does not wait this way.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: Already settled by running the program. A measurement on a real cartridge would confirm it.

divergences.referenceDoes: Gives the enable bit, the two register addresses and the size of the shared window.
divergences.reasoning: Running the microcode settles what the part computes and settles nothing about where the console reaches it. Those constants come from a reference and from the cartridge drivers that use them, which is the weakest evidence in this package and sits underneath everything else in it.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A cartridge board schematic, a continuity reading, or a die photograph.

divergences.referenceDoes: Often treats the two as one part with two images.
divergences.reasoning: They are not the same. The ST010 watches words 3, 4 and 5 while it waits and the ST011 watches word 2, and each was measured by running its own program rather than assumed from the other. Assuming would have made one of the two silently wrong in a way that only shows on a cartridge nobody tested.
divergences.wouldReopenIt: A third image whose wait differs again, which would mean the pattern is per image rather than per part.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: Already settled by running each program.

divergences.reasoning: The microcode belongs to whoever made the part. What is carried is a manifest: the length and four digests of each image, with SHA-256 deciding. A file that does not match is refused rather than run, because running the wrong image would report behaviour no hardware has.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: n/a. This is a boundary rather than an unknown.

divergences.documentSays: The uPD77C25 data sheet gives one instruction per clock for the smaller part.
divergences.referenceDoes: Answers immediately: the reference implementations run a started command to its end inside the write that starts it.
divergences.reasoning: A started command now runs on the processor's clock: the start write only stores the bit, a polling console reads the part busy, and finish() reports the instructions the microcode took. What is still not modelled is how long an instruction lasts. fullsnes, fetched 2026-10-19 with SHA-256 3853b65a7331bf12eea431ff494a2948a1c78ef22f7e819db4b139fd5a79f6c6, reads the oscillators off the boards as a 22.000 MHz [M]22000C on the ST010 and a 15.000 MHz 15.00X on the ST011, so the crystal is known from a third-party board reading. How many oscillator periods one uPD96050 instruction costs is not: the uPD77C25 takes one external clock per instruction, nobody has a uPD96050 document, and fullsnes's internal 11.000 MHz for the ST010 comes with no measurement.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A uPD96050 data sheet, or a command timed on a real cartridge in console cycles and divided by the instruction count finish() reports.

divergences.documentSays: Nothing. No document for this part exists.
divergences.referenceDoes: ares owns the bit in its own bridge, as a flag neither side writes.
divergences.reasoning: Both halves of the mailbox were read off artifacts and they pair: the console writes $3802 and the part reads 0x40000010, the part writes 0x40000000 and the console reads $3800, each gated by one bit of a status register the other side never touches. A third pair was found on 2026-10-20: the firmware stores a byte at 0x40000010, at 0x000470, and the cartridge polls bit 2 of $3804 at $E806 and then reads $3802 at $E812, discarding the value; ares sets bit 2 on that store and clears it on that read, answering 0, and this package does the same. Bit 7 of $3804 is the exception. The cartridge polls it after the reset pulse and no instruction in the firmware sets it, so it is the interface hardware answering rather than the program. This package raises it when the part is reset, which is what makes the part usable and is not something either artifact says. An independent implementation does the same, which is consistent and is not evidence: an implementation is free to invent a flag that satisfies the firmware it was tested against. The two guard bits are the same shape and are named in st018.py and never set, because setting them would be a claim.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: The package opened and the interface probed. There is no bus to reach it on: the ROM is on the die and the interface is inside the same package.
divergences.wouldReopenIt: A document for this part, which nobody has published.

divergences.documentSays: Nothing. Seta published nothing about either part.
divergences.referenceDoes: Reference implementations start a command on a write to $680021, which is what the microcode waits on rather than something a driver was read for.
divergences.reasoning: The static readings never reached a write to $680021, and the record said every write to the pair was one byte wide. Running the cartridge showed otherwise. The ST010 image Exhaust Heat II - F1 Driver e no Michi (Japan), SHA-256 1c78d8208a05cbfe88ee019edbc3a0c9cdabfd2b62089ca119215bbc7e581611, run headless in MAME 0.289 with a write tap on $680000-$6FFFFF, wrote $06 to $680020 and $80 to $680021 from one instruction at $80:8D69, frame 992 of the attract run. Its bytes at file offset 0x0D66 are A9 06 80 8F 20 00 68: a sixteen bit load of $8006 and a long store to $680020, so the start is a word-wide write whose high byte carries the start bit, and all nine long stores to $680020 in the image are preceded by A9 nn 80. The snes-driver-python reader lost the accumulator width at these sites; re-recorded on 2026-10-19 from that reader at adc1b8c, the ST010 shapes carry write2~@0x680020 wherever its MAME trace saw the word store. The ST011 image, Hayazashi Nidan Morita Shougi (Japan), SHA-256 85825a75ef662b28d0111c0462ec3c34234da1d78d10472b8022fcba3b9eaed5, run the same way for 600 seconds with buttons pressed in turn, wrote only the data port at $600000 and never $680000-$68017F, and holds no long store to the pair.
wouldSettleIt: for the ST011, a run that reaches the shogi engine's moves while watching $680021 and $600000
a capture of a real console driving the ST011
divergences.wouldReopenIt: An ST010 site that starts a command some other way than a word write of $80nn to $680020.

divergences.documentSays: Nothing. An access's width is the accumulator's width when the cartridge's routine runs, which whoever called the routine set.
divergences.referenceDoes: snes-driver-python reads each width from the code where the code sets it, from a run where one used it, marked *, from a headless MAME trace of the cartridge, marked ~, and otherwise reports it as ?.
divergences.reasoning: Every recorded shape is kept and every width carries its label; a ? is replayed as one byte, as every width was before the label existed, and conformance.against_cartridges counts the accesses that rest on that assumption. Measured on 2026-10-20 from the reader at 62d619b, which walks both arms of every forward conditional branch: 21 of 42 ST010 shapes and 10 of 16 ST011 shapes carry a ?, 92 of 232 and 30 of 76 accesses counted as often as each shape was seen. The 1,543 ST018 shapes are all known.
wouldSettleIt: a trace that reaches the routine an assumed width sits in
a jump table the reader's walk can follow to that routine's callers

divergences.documentSays: Nothing. No document for this part exists.
divergences.referenceDoes: ares at commit 9408cb43d4948fc3ea6e152a307a34348df3fe04, sfc/coprocessor/armdsp/memory.cpp and armdsp.cpp: writes to 0x40000020, 0x40000024 and 0x40000028 set bytes 0, 1 and 2 of a latch, a write to 0x4000002C copies the latch into a 32-bit count, every call to step(1), which ares makes once per ARM bus access or idle cycle, lowers a nonzero count by one, and a reset clears both. Nothing in ares reads the count.
divergences.reasoning: The firmware writes those four ports in that order, which is the artifact's evidence, and an earlier version of this model kept only the byte written to 0x20 and never counted. Following the one independent implementation turns a stored byte into a timer that runs on the ARM's own cycles, at the rung of that implementation rather than of the part. Nothing observable depends on it yet: the status byte does not carry it and no instruction the firmware was seen to execute reads it back.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: The firmware reading the count, or a line the count drives, observed on a real part, or a document for the part.
divergences.wouldReopenIt: A later ares or another implementation that reads the count back or lets it raise an interrupt.
